sbh1.3:1.0: The source has *naiṣkramyabhūmiḥ naiṣkramyabhūmiḥ katamā* — the bhūmi name repeated, with no Roman-numeral marker. Treated here as 'name + question': the first occurrence (now :1.0) functions as the section header (as Roman-numeral *I.* and *II.* did in [sbh1.1](sbh1.1.html) and [sbh1.2](sbh1.2.html)), the second (now :1.1) as the standard *X katamā* opening question. The Roman numeral *III.* has been editorially restored in brackets — the dittographic doubling of *naiṣkramyabhūmiḥ* in the source likely covers a lost *III.* marker, since the section is the third sub-bhūmi of Yogasthāna I in clear continuity with the *I.*/*II.* pattern of the preceding two.
sbh1.3:1.8: *samāpatti-upapattika dhyāna* — the dhyāna treated under both its aspects: as a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) reached in this life, and as a corresponding mode of rebirth (*upapatti*) into the dhyāna-heaven of the same name. This dual reference is canonical: the same term names both the practice and the cosmological-rebirth realm it leads to.
sbh1.3:1.9: *satkāya-vairāgyam* — 'dispassion toward the personality.' In context, the practitioner attains dispassion specifically toward the *kāmadhātu*-bound personality — the embodied-self of the desire realm — which is the precondition for transitioning into the first dhyāna. *Satkāya* (literally 'existing body / aggregates') is the same term that grounds *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (identity-view).
sbh1.3:1.21: *darśana-bhāvanā-prahātavyebhyo dharmebhyaḥ* — 'the dharmas to be abandoned by vision and by cultivation.' Refers to the canonical two-stage path of the *darśana-mārga* (path of seeing, which abandons the intellectually-grasped defilements at first true insight) and the *bhāvanā-mārga* (path of cultivation, which gradually wears down the residual affective defilements). Together these constitute the supramundane path proper.
sbh1.3:2.3: The list enumerates the thirteen *saṁbhāra* (requisites) that the rest of this chapter unpacks. Compare the closing *uddāna* verse at sbh1.3:80–81 for the canonical summary order. *Kalyāṇamitratā* (association with good friends) appears in this enumeration but is folded into [*parasampat*](sbh1.1.html#sbh1.1:1.26) in the gotrabhūmi treatment, hence its absence from the closing verse.
sbh1.3:2.5: Cross-reference back to [sbh1.1:10.20–21](sbh1.1.html#sbh1.1:10.20), the gotrabhūmi treatment of *ātmasampat*, *parasampat*, and *kuśala-dharma-cchanda* under the rubric of the lesser supporting condition for the perfecting of the lineage-seed. The avatārabhūmi does not re-define these three; the present chapter inherits them and proceeds directly to the fourth requisite (*śīla-saṁvara*) at 2.6.
sbh1.3:80.1: The closing *uddāna* (summary verse) is in *śloka* meter; English here drops the meter and adds bracketed clarifications so the verse remains a list-pointer rather than a freestanding statement. Verses 80–81 enumerate the twelve saṁbhāras of the chapter (with *kalyāṇamitratā* implicit under *parasampat*); verses 82–83 enumerate the qualities of the recluse-ornament treated in sections 71–78.
sbh1.3:3.2: *sapta-naiḥsaraṇika śīla-skandha* — the seven categories of virtue conducive to liberation (*naiḥsaraṇika*, 'leading-out'). The Yogācāra schema enumerates the seven kinds of Prātimokṣa-restraint (bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, upāsaka, upāsikā). The clause 'taking the monastic restraint specifically' (3.4) signals that this whole chapter operates within the bhikṣu's full ordination, even though the underlying *śīla-skandha* is structurally broader.
sbh1.3:5.14: *jñapti-caturtha karman* — the 'fourth-formal-motion act,' the standard Vinaya procedure by which full ordination is conferred. The proposer states the motion (*jñapti*) and then three times asks the assembled saṅgha to confirm; silence on all three counts conveys consent. The phrasing here makes the point that at ordination the candidate hears only the framework of the precepts — the full hundred-odd training rules are received under pledge (*samādāna-pratijñā*) and gradually awakened to over the course of training, which is the work of section 5 as a whole.
sbh1.3:8.6: *niḥsaraṇa-śīla* — 'outgoing-virtue,' i.e., virtue that *leads out* (of saṁsāra). The text triangulates the three trainings: Prātimokṣa-restraint *is* the higher-virtue training (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), which serves as forerunner for the higher-mind (*adhicitta*) and higher-wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) trainings that complete the path. The term *niḥsaraṇa* (with cognate *naiḥsaraṇika* at 3.2) recurs as the standard Yogācāra marker of soteriological efficacy.
sbh1.3:11.28: The list — *kuhanā* (hypocrisy), *lapanā* (talkative chatter), *naimittikatā* (insinuating hints), *naiṣpeṣikatā* (extortion / pressing), and *lābhena lābha-niścikīrṣā* (seeking gain by means of gain) — is the canonical *pañca-mithyā-jīva*, the five wrong livelihoods of monastics. Standard list across both Theravāda Visuddhimagga (I.61) and Sarvāstivāda-Yogācāra abhidharma; preserved here in brackets so the reader can recognize the technical taxonomy underneath the long descriptive expansions at 11.15–27.
sbh1.3:37.2: The three-fold danger schema (consumption / transformation / seeking, *pariniṣpatti / pariṇāma / paryeṣaṇa*) is a canonical Yogācāra analysis of food's faults. The seeking-danger then subdivides into six sub-types (37.31–35) — gathering, guarding, loss-of-affection, insatiability, lack-of-independence, misconduct — which structurally parallel the well-known *kāma-ādīnava* (drawbacks of sense-pleasures) lists in the Pāli Mahādukkhakkhandha-sutta (MN 13).
sbh1.3:39.48: The four kinds of food (*catur āhāra*) — morsel-made (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), contact (*sparśa*), mental volition (*manaḥsaṁcetanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) — is canonical abhidharma. The text narrows the *bhojane mātrajñatā* discussion to the first only, *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* — actual physical food taken by the body. The other three are subtle nutriments that sustain saṁsāric continuity at deeper levels.
sbh1.3:39.90: *aniṣṭha-prahāṇa* — literally 'abandonment by non-establishment.' The point is that for food, the practitioner does not abandon by ceasing-to-use (impossible while embodied); rather, he abandons attachment to it while continuing the physical act of eating. The phrase is technical: this is the same abandonment-without-cessation that recurs for the *requisite-items* (*pariṣkāra*) generally, where the bodily activity must continue but the affective grip on it must be released.
sbh1.3:40.90: *bhojane mātrajña* — 'knowing the right measure in food.' The term *mātra* ('measure') is glossed concretely by the analysis at 40.59–74: balanced (*sama*) versus unbalanced (*viṣama*) eating, where balanced cuts across four dimensions — quantity (not too little, not too much), digestibility, wholesomeness, and freedom-from-defilement-in-procurement. The Vinaya formula *paryāptaṁ* (sufficient) and *yathāpramāṇa* (according to measure) point to the same idea.
sbh1.3:42.95: The three *ādhipateyya* (predominances) — dharma-, self-, and world-predominance — is a canonical Yogācāra schema applied to motivation for abandoning the hindrances. Dharma-predominance (42.21–94) is the practitioner's own analytical work with antidotes; self-predominance (42.97–100) is the motive of self-respect ('let me not be known as a hindrance-maker'); world-predominance (42.101–108) is the motive of accountability before the Teacher, the deities, the wise, and the saṅgha. The threefold framework reappears in the Yogācārabhūmi as the standard motivational analysis whenever a single practice has multiple subjective angles.
sbh1.3:42.176: The four *samyak-prayoga* (right tasks) of wakefulness-yoga — sustained wholesome practice while awake, sleeping at the right time, sleeping with undefiled mind, [and] waking at the right time — are paired (42.187–204) one-to-one with the four phrases of the canonical wakefulness-formula (purifies-by-walking-and-sitting / lies-down-foot-on-foot / mindful-and-fully-aware / wakes-in-the-last-watch). This pairing is a Yogācāra hermeneutic technique: a brief sūtra-formula is fully unfolded by mapping each phrase onto a named element of a corresponding doctrinal list.
sbh1.3:42.218: *saṁprajāna-vihāritā* (dwelling-with-full-awareness) is introduced here as a transition into the next major topic (paragraphs 43–54 develop it in detail). Within the wakefulness-yoga, *saṁprajāna* names the moment-by-moment monitoring of bodily and mental activity during all four postures (the four *īryāpatha*). The placement at 42.218 — at the end of the wakefulness section — signals that wakefulness and full-awareness are continuous and overlapping: wakefulness-yoga is the temporal frame (when), saṁprajāna is the qualitative texture (how).
sbh1.3:47.1: Although the chapter heading at 42.218 introduces *saṁprajāna-vihāritā*, paragraphs 47–54 actually open the next saṁbhāra — *kalyāṇa-mitratā* (association with good friends) — by detailing the conduct on the alms-round and in solitary practice (47–50) and then enumerating the eight qualities (51–52) and four roles (53) of the good friend himself, closing with the summary at 54.1. The two topics are bridged because what one learns through *saṁprajāna* in daily activity is precisely the conduct *modeled* by the *kalyāṇa-mitra*.
sbh1.3:51.7: The four-fold characterization of the good friend — much-learned (*bahuśruta*), attainer (*samāpatti-lābhin*), compassionate (*kṛpālu*), and of unwearying mind (*akhinna-mānasa*) — followed by patience, confidence, and speech-faculty at 51.25–52.11, yields the eight causes/aspects named at 52.12 and again at 53.51. This same eight-fold list is canonical for *kalyāṇa-mitra* across Yogācāra sources. The 'three wonders' at 51.12–13 (*prātihārya*: psychic power, mind-reading, admonition) match the standard Pāli list of *iddhi/ādesanā/anuśāsanī*-pāṭihāriya from DN 11 and elsewhere.
sbh1.3:53.31: The list of twelve *kathā-vastu* (topics of discourse) — virtue-talk, wisdom-talk, liberation-talk, few-desires-talk, knowing-and-seeing-of-liberation-talk, contentment-talk, abandonment-talk, dispassion-talk, cessation-talk, decrease-talk [*apacaya*], non-mixing-talk [*asaṁsarga*], pratītyasamutpāda-conforming-talk — is the canonical *dvādaśa-kathā-vastu* of Yogācāra abhidharma. Cf. the ten-fold *kathā-vatthu* list in the Pāli Anguttara (AN 10.69).
sbh1.3:72.60: The twelve (or thirteen) *dhutaguṇa* — *paiṇḍapātika, sāpadāna-cārin, aikāsanika, khalupaścādbhaktika, traicīvarika, nāmatika, pāṁsukūlika, āraṇyaka, vṛkṣamūlika, ābhyavakāśika, śmāśānika, naiṣadika, yāthāsaṁstarika* — match the Pāli *dhutaṅga* list of the Visuddhimagga II, with terminology and ordering essentially identical. The Yogācāra count of thirteen treats *piṇḍapāta* and *sāpadāna-cāra* as distinct; the count of twelve subsumes the second under the first. The functional analysis at 78.1–16 maps each dhutaguṇa onto the specific kind of lust (*rāga*) it counteracts — a Yogācāra abhidharma move that converts the ascetic list from a catalogue of practices into a typology of antidotes.
sbh1.3:77.10: The folk-etymology *dhuta-guṇa* ← *dhuta* (shaken, shaken-off): just as wool/cotton becomes loose and workable when shaken, so the mind becomes loose and workable when 'shaken' free of attachment to food, robes, and lodging through these ascetic disciplines. The simile is also found in the Visuddhimagga and is the standard explanation across Buddhist sects for why these are called 'dhutaguṇa.'
sbh1.3:78.48: The *ṣaṭ-sāmīcī-dharma* (six conciliatory dharmas) — friendly bodily action, friendly verbal action, friendly mental action, sharing in gains (open-eating at meals), sharing in virtue [*śīla-sāmānyatā*], and sharing in view [*dṛṣṭi-sāmānyatā*] — are the standard list of the six *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (Pāli) / *sāmīcī-dharma* (Skt.) of conciliatory living. Identical in Pāli AN 6.11–12 and across Yogācāra sources, defining the conditions of harmonious *saṅgha* life.
sbh1.3:78.97: The closing simile — the well-adorned young man — picks up and inverts the *ornament*-simile from 12.22–29 (where virtue is contrasted with worldly ornaments that fail in old age and misfortune): there, worldly ornaments fail and only virtue endures; here, the worldly ornament *succeeds* as a comparison-vehicle precisely because the disciple's recluse-ornament is its true, non-decaying analogue. The two passages function as inclusio at the opening and close of the saṁbhāra-section.
sbh1.3:84.1: Closing colophon for the entire Yogasthāna I — not just the naiṣkramyabhūmi. The Sanskrit accusative *prathamaṁ yogasthānaṁ* leaves the verb implicit (*samāptam*, 'is completed'); rendered here with a bracketed gloss. The same colophon-form repeats at the close of YS II, III, and IV in the source.
sbh1.3:32.17: The four-term cluster *nityakāritā / sātatya-kāritā / niryāṇa-kāritā / satkṛtya-kāritā* — 'constant action / continual action / action toward going-forth / action done with respect' — pairs each term in the question (32.15–16) with its definitional synonym (32.17–18). The Sanskrit *iyam ucyate X* construction here re-glosses the question's term, so 'constant' is *defined as* 'continual' and 'going-forth' is *defined as* 'with-respect'. Translation makes the pairing explicit so the reader can see the gloss structure rather than reading 32.17–18 as separate vague claims.
sbh1.3:32.38: *samāvasthā-avacāraka* — literally 'one who explores / operates within an even state.' Rendered here as 'one who maintains a balanced state.' The earlier draft used 'acting in the state of equipoise,' which is technically defensible but sounded liturgical; 'balanced state' carries the same conceptual content with less ornament. Distinct from *upekṣā* (equanimity) proper — *upekṣā* names the affective neutrality, *samāvasthā-avacāraka* names the stable mode of operating from within it.
sbh1.3:35.50: The twofold distinction here is doctrinally important: *pratisaṁkhyāna-bala* (the power of reflective discrimination) is the analytical force that *recognizes* danger in sense-objects without yet uprooting it; *bhāvanā-bala* (the power of cultivation) actually uproots the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) at its karmic root. The first kind belongs to the path of requisites (*saṁbhāra-mārga*) — pre-realization. The second is operative within the dispassion-stage proper, i.e., from the path of seeing onward.
sbh1.3:55.16: *geya* (sung-verse) and *vyākaraṇa* (predictive teaching) are paired in 55.16–20 with two contrasting kinds of sūtra: *neyārtha* (meaning-to-be-interpreted) sūtras paired with *geya*, and *nītārtha* (definitive-meaning) sūtras paired with *vyākaraṇa*. The pairing is structural and tradition-recognized in the twelve-aṅga schema; preserved here in brackets for visibility.
sbh1.3:60.4: The mapping of the twelve *aṅgas* (verbal genres) onto the three *piṭakas* (baskets) given here is a Yogācāra schema: ten aṅgas (sūtra through adbhutadharma) constitute the *sūtra-piṭaka*; *nidāna* alone constitutes the *vinaya-piṭaka* (since vinaya rules are framed by their occasioning narratives); *upadeśa* constitutes the *abhidharma-piṭaka*. Different traditions (Theravāda, etc.) assign these differently.
sbh1.3:60.30: The six *acintya-sthāna* (unthinkable matters) — self, being, world, the karmic results of beings, the meditator's range as known to meditators, and the Buddha's range as known to Buddhas — are explicitly *set aside* before reflection begins. The reflection that constitutes *cintanā* operates on what *can* be analytically known: dharma's own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general-characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
sbh1.3:61.2: The four reasonings (*yukti*) introduced at 60.44 — *apekṣā* (dependence), *kāryakāraṇa* (cause-effect), *upapatti-sādhana* (demonstration-of-arising), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) — are a canonical Yogācāra fourfold, expanded in section 61. Compare the four-reasoning treatment in [sbh3.2](sbh3.2.html#sbh3.2:0.2) (vipaśyanā), where they reappear as the analytical engines of insight.
sbh1.3:62.4: *anantarāya* is defined here by negation: the discussion (62.7–62.30) details the *obstacles* (*antarāya*); *non-obstacle* is then implied as their absence. This negative-definition pattern is common in the Śrāvakabhūmi when the positive content has already been laid out elsewhere or is best understood by contrast.
sbh1.3:63.2: The threefold division of obstacle is structurally important: *prayoga-antarāya* obstructs the *application* itself (illness, lack of basic requisites); *prāvivekya-antarāya* obstructs the *seclusion* in which application happens (busy-ness, sociability, distraction); *pratisaṁlayana-antarāya* obstructs *retreat* — the inner work of śamatha and vipaśyanā — through heedlessness, premature settling, self-aggrandizement, or fickleness. The categories cascade from gross-and-environmental to subtle-and-internal.
sbh1.3:64.3: The six-question framework — who, to whom, what, by what, how, why — is the standard Yogācāra analytical schema applied to any practice (also visible in the *kena/kiṁ/kutaḥ/kathaṁ* framing of indriya-saṁvara at 35.16–18). Sections 65–70 answer each question in turn: 65 = giver-and-recipients; 67–69 = the thing given (sentient and non-sentient); 70 = means, manner, motive.
sbh1.3:65.3: *dātṛ* (giver) and *dāna-pati* (patron) are distinguished: anyone whose own thing is given is a giver; the patron is specifically the one who gives *willingly*. The distinction matters because one can be a giver under coercion (e.g., taxation, theft) without being a patron; only the willing giver is a patron, and only the willing giving constitutes the *tyāga* requisite.
sbh1.3:67.8: Self-giving (offering parts of one's own body — head, hand, flesh, blood) is here explicitly *bracketed off* as a bodhisattva practice that is not the *tyāga* requisite intended in the śrāvakabhūmi context. This is one of the few places where the source explicitly demarcates between śrāvaka and bodhisattva paths within a discussion that could apply to either.
